title: Five Extra Minutes of Sleep and Two Minutes of Exercise a Day Could Add a Full Year to Your Life
excerpt: A landmark UK Biobank study of nearly 60,000 adults finds that tiny, simultaneous improvements in sleep, physical activity, and diet compound into as much as 9.4 extra years of disease-free living — and the findings carry outsized implications for South Asians.
body:
Most health advice asks you to overhaul one thing at a time: run more, eat better, sleep longer. But a sweeping new study published in *The Lancet eClinicalMedicine* suggests the real power lies not in dramatic changes to any single habit, but in making small improvements to all three at once.

Researchers at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre tracked 59,078 adults from the UK Biobank using wrist-worn accelerometers and comprehensive dietary surveys over a median follow-up of 8.1 years. Their question was deceptively simple: what is the *minimum* combined change in sleep, physical activity, and nutrition (which the researchers call "SPAN") needed to meaningfully extend life?

## The Smallest Dose That Makes a Difference

The numbers are striking in their modesty. An additional five minutes of sleep per night, just two minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise per day, and a five-point improvement in diet quality — roughly equivalent to adding half a serving of vegetables — was associated with one full additional year of life.

Scale those improvements up slightly — to 24 extra minutes of sleep, about four minutes more of exercise, and a meaningfully better diet (an extra cup of vegetables plus two servings of fish per week) — and the study found an association with four additional years of *healthspan*, defined as years lived free of cardiovascular disease, cancer, type 2 diabetes, COPD, and dementia.

At the optimal end of the spectrum, participants who slept 7.2 to 8.0 hours per night, exercised at moderate-to-vigorous intensity for more than 42 minutes per day, and ate a high-quality diet enjoyed 9.35 additional years of lifespan and 9.45 years of healthspan compared to those in the lowest tier for all three behaviours.

## Why Combined Changes Beat Single Habits



> **"Their question was deceptively simple: what is the *minimum* combined change in sleep, physical activity, and nutrition (which the researchers call "SPAN") needed to meaningfully extend life?"**


The study's most important insight may be its demonstration of synergy. When the researchers examined each behaviour in isolation, the amount of change needed for a meaningful reduction in mortality risk was much higher. Sleep alone required 60 per cent more improvement (24 extra minutes, not five) to achieve the same benefit. Diet quality alone could not achieve a statistically significant reduction in mortality at any dose.

"When SPAN behaviours are targeted concurrently, even subtle variations may be associated with significant long-term cardiovascular benefits," the researchers wrote in a companion study published in the *European Heart Journal*, which found the optimal SPAN combination was associated with a 57 per cent lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events.

The biological logic is well established. Sleep deprivation disrupts appetite hormones, leading to overeating. Poor diet reduces sleep quality. Fatigue from short sleep discourages physical activity. These behaviours are interdependent — and so are their benefits when improved together.


![Charles Perkins Centre — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Charles_Perkins_Centre%2C_University_of_Sydney.jpg/3840px-Charles_Perkins_Centre%2C_University_of_Sydney.jpg)


## What This Means for the South Asian Diaspora

For Indians and South Asians abroad, these findings carry particular weight. South Asians experience disproportionately high rates of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome — often at lower body mass indexes than other populations. A 2026 clinical practice statement from the American Society for Preventive Cardiology highlighted that culturally tailored lifestyle interventions are essential for effective cardiometabolic risk reduction in this community.

The challenge for many diaspora professionals is not ignorance of health risks but the practical difficulty of making large lifestyle changes while managing demanding careers, long commutes, and family responsibilities across time zones. The SPAN study's central message — that the threshold for meaningful benefit is remarkably low — offers a pragmatic counter to the all-or-nothing mindset that often accompanies wellness advice.

Adding two minutes of brisk walking to an existing commute, going to bed five minutes earlier, and adding a handful of spinach to an evening dal may sound trivial. But the data suggest these micro-shifts, when stacked together, set off a cascade of reduced inflammation, better glycaemic control, and lower blood pressure that compounds over years.

## The Science of "Good Enough"

The study used accelerometer data rather than self-reported exercise logs, which gives the findings greater precision than most prior lifestyle research. It also explicitly modelled healthspan — not just lifespan — tracking whether participants developed any of five major chronic diseases, not just whether they survived.

The authors caution that the findings are observational and reflect theoretical relationships, not proven interventions. A randomised trial called SPIRAL+, currently underway in France, is testing whether a combined sleep-exercise-diet programme produces the real-world health gains the SPAN data predict.

But the direction of the evidence is now hard to ignore. As the researchers put it: "Small, concurrent improvements in sleep, physical activity, and diet quality were associated with clinically meaningful gains in lifespan and healthspan."

For a community where cardiovascular risk runs high and cultural food traditions can both help (lentils, vegetables, fish) and hinder (refined carbohydrates, fried snacks), the takeaway is both hopeful and specific. You do not need to train for a marathon, adopt a radical diet, or restructure your entire evening routine. You need to do a little more of three things at the same time.

**Sources:** *The Lancet eClinicalMedicine* (Koemel et al., 2026); *BMC Medicine* (Koemel et al., 2025); *European Heart Journal* (Koemel et al., 2026); American Society for Preventive Cardiology clinical practice statement on South Asian cardiometabolic health (2025).
